rationale: There is no longitudinal or quantitative neuroimaging evidence supporting a stereotyped anatomical sequence in SPAX11 where vermian atrophy precedes hemispheric atrophy by at least five years. In the definitive clinical report describing SPAX11 (OMIM #621226) caused by the TUBA4A p.Glu415Lys variant (Torella et al., 2023), brain MRI demonstrated only 'slight or absent cerebellar atrophy' and 'questionable upper vermis atrophy'. No systematic five-year latency between vermian and hemispheric loss has ever been observed or documented.

evidence.text: Brain MRI in individuals with TUBA4A-associated spastic ataxia demonstrated slight or absent cerebellar atrophy, with only questionable upper vermis atrophy noted, rather than progressive longitudinal volumetric stages.

source.title: A new genetic cause of spastic ataxia: the p.Glu415Lys variant in TUBA4A

evidence.text: Clinical synopsis and entry for SPAX11 confirms that brain MRI findings are limited to questionable atrophy of the upper vermis without documenting a five-year sequence preceding hemispheric atrophy.

conflicts: The hypothesis asserts a proven 5-year chronological progression from vermian to hemispheric atrophy, whereas clinical reports describe imaging findings merely as 'slight or absent cerebellar atrophy' with 'questionable upper vermis atrophy'.

new_directions.question_text: What are the quantitative volumetric MRI trajectories of the cerebellar vermis versus hemispheres in longitudinal follow-ups of TUBA4A mutation carriers?
new_directions.rationale: SPAX11 has only recently been defined in two kindreds; serial volumetric 3D T1 MRI data are required to establish whether true cerebellar volume loss occurs and whether it follows a regional gradient.

new_directions.question_text: Does neurofilament light chain (NfL) elevation precede or correlate with detectable neuroimaging changes in presymptomatic or early symptomatic TUBA4A p.Glu415Lys carriers?
new_directions.rationale: Establishing fluid biomarker timelines will resolve whether axonal damage occurs well before subtle vermian or cerebellar changes can be reliably identified on neuroimaging.
